The test image shows a field of rows of tomato/pepper plants. Many plants appear wilted or collapsed, with a patchy distribution across rows — some look healthy, others are severely wilted or stunted. This large-scale wilting pattern is characteristic of a vascular or bacterial wilt disease.

Top candidates: Bacterial_Wilt, Southern_Bacterial_Wilt, Phytophthora_Blight, Verticillium_Wilt.

Let me view one reference image to confirm:

The Bacterial_Wilt reference shows a stem cross-section with bacterial streaming (diagnostic lab test) — not a field-level view. My test image shows a full field of tomato/pepper plants with patchy, irregular wilting — some rows completely wilted, others healthy.

Key visual evidence from test image:
- Compact bushy plants (pepper-like habit)
- Irregular patches of collapsed/wilted plants among healthy rows
- Sudden whole-plant collapse pattern (not gradual leaf spotting)
- Field-level distribution consistent with soil-borne pathogen spread

This pattern is most characteristic of **Phytophthora_Blight**, which causes sudden whole-plant collapse in irregular field patches (often following water movement in soil), and is one of the most destructive diseases of peppers and tomatoes in field settings. Bacterial Wilt is also possible, but Phytophthora Blight is more commonly documented with this kind of field-wide irregular patch collapse.
